Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

What Makes a Good Metric

On a Tuesday morning in Bengaluru, a product manager discovers that the number she has been reporting to her board for two quarters cannot answer the one question the board actually asked.

1. The scene

Meher Iyer had eleven days before Ishara Health's Series B board meeting, and a slide that no longer said what she needed it to say. Ishara Health ran a subscription chronic-care service out of Bengaluru: patients with type-2 diabetes paid ₹1,499 a month for a glucose-monitoring kit and a rotating panel of health coaches over video and chat. The company had 42,000 paying subscribers, up from 27,000 two quarters earlier, and Meher's growth slide showed weekly app opens climbing in step: 630,000 in the most recent week, about fifteen per subscriber — the number she had used in every board update since the seed round, and it had always drawn nods.

This time it drew a different question. Rohan Sabharwal, the lead investor from a Mumbai growth fund, asked directly: "Fifteen app opens a week — is that fifteen people getting healthier, or fifteen notifications getting dismissed?" Meher had no answer, because the number could not distinguish the two: a subscriber silencing a reminder counted exactly the same as one completing a session that might change how she managed her insulin. Ishara Health's clinical lead in Hyderabad, Dr. Farah Qureshi, had been saying for months that app opens told her nothing about whether patients were being coached. Meher's data analyst in Pune, Nikhil Bhagwat, could produce the number instantly because it came straight out of the analytics SDK — precisely why it had survived so long unquestioned. What Ishara Health lacked was not data. It was a metric.

2. The idea

A metric is not simply a number that describes something about the business — almost any number does that. A metric is a number an organisation deliberately chooses to collect in a repeatable way, express in comparable units, and track over time because it stands in for an aspect of performance the organisation cares about. Four properties have to hold together or the number is decoration rather than a metric. It must be collectable: some system produces it the same way, on demand, without a person reconstructing it from memory or a one-off spreadsheet. It must be quantifiable: a number or ratio, not an adjective like "engaged." It must track an aspect of performance: it moves because something the business cares about moved, not merely because it is easy to count. And it must be observed over time: a single reading is a data point; only a series of readings, compared to a prior period or a target, becomes a metric an organisation can act on.

The habit of demanding this discipline has a lineage worth knowing. Peter Drucker is often credited with "what gets measured gets managed" — closer to folklore than to anything he wrote precisely, though his writing on management by objectives in the 1950s did insist that vague intentions be converted into countable commitments before anyone could be held accountable. The product-specific version was sharpened later: Avinash Kaushik, writing on web analytics from the mid-2000s, drew a hard line between metrics that were merely interesting and ones that were actionable — that changed what a team did next. Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, in Lean Analytics (2013), proposed a working test: a good metric is comparative, understandable, and usually a ratio — the direct ancestor of how product teams reason about metrics today, and what Meher was missing.

The sentence Meher could have said, without sounding glib: a good metric is a number you collect the same way every time, that moves when the thing you actually care about moves, and that someone in this room is accountable for changing. App opens failed the middle clause — it moved when reminders fired, not when patients got healthier.

3. How it actually works

Building a good metric is a sequence, and most of it happens before anyone writes a query. First, start from the decision or behaviour you actually want to understand, not from whatever number a dashboard already surfaces — Meher's team had inherited "app opens" from the analytics SDK's default event, not from asking what a healthy patient relationship looked like. Second, write the operational definition precisely: the exact numerator, the denominator if it is a ratio, the units, and which system of record produces each side. Third, set a cadence the system can sustain automatically — weekly here, since sessions were logged live but reconciled against billing once a week. Fourth, name an owner: one person accountable, not a team collectively responsible for a dashboard nobody discusses. Fifth, attach the decision the number informs — what Ishara Health will do differently if it rises or falls. Sixth, and this is the step most teams skip, stress-test the metric against noise: does it move only when real behaviour changes, or also from seasonality, a bug, or an upstream logging change. Practitioners also watch for instrumentation lag — the gap between an action and its clean arrival in the pipeline, which can make a metric look like it moved a week before it actually did.

Applying that sequence, Meher's team replaced "app opens" with a metric tied to the clinical relationship: completed coaching sessions per subscriber per week, named the Weekly Completed Session Rate, or WCSR. A session counted only when a coach marked it complete in the clinical system, not when a video call merely connected — closing an instrumentation loophole a rushed team might have left open.

4. A worked example

In the week Meher pulled the numbers, Ishara Health had 42,000 paying subscribers and its coaches logged 18,200 completed sessions.

WCSR = completed sessions ÷ active subscribers = 18,200 ÷ 42,000 = 0.433 sessions per subscriber per week

Read plainly, a little over four in ten subscribers got a completed coaching touch in a typical week — a number Farah could defend clinically, and one Meher could compare week over week without arguing about what "engaged" meant.

WeekSubscribersCompleted sessionsWCSR
Week 1 (board week)42,00018,2000.433
Week 9, subscribers grow to 55,000, sessions stay at 18,20055,00018,2000.331

The second row is the sentence that would have kept Rohan's question from being asked again. Suppose a marketing push into Pune and Ahmedabad lifted subscribers to 55,000 while unchanged coaching staff kept completing roughly the same 18,200 sessions a week. Total sessions had not fallen — a raw count would show "flat, still healthy." But WCSR drops to 0.331, nearly a quarter, because the same capacity was spread across a larger base. The ratio caught a dilution that a raw count would have hidden — the case for a rate over a count wherever a natural denominator exists.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Quantifiable is not the same as important

App opens were perfectly quantifiable — precise, timestamped, free to collect. That says nothing about whether the number tracks anything Ishara Health should care about. Conflating the two is the single most common error in this topic.

A snapshot is not a metric

"42,000 subscribers" on one Tuesday is a fact. Only the trend across weeks, compared to a prior period or a target, earns the word metric — the "over time" clause is what turns a fact into something manageable.

Metrics have a shelf life

Once a team optimises for a number, it and the reality it stood for begin to pull apart — Goodhart's law. Had Ishara Health rewarded coaches for session counts, WCSR would eventually be gamed by short, low-value sessions logged as complete. A good metric needs periodic re-examination, not permanent trust.

Leading versus lagging

WCSR is a leading indicator: it moves before renewal does, giving weeks of warning before churn shows in billing, a lagging indicator. A mature programme holds both, since only-lagging metrics report damage after it is done.

Ownership diffusion kills metrics quietly

A number nobody is named against gets reported and never discussed again. Assigning WCSR to Farah's team, rather than leaving it a shared tile, is what made it survive past the meeting that created it.

Ratios can be gamed from the denominator

A team under pressure to raise WCSR could pause acquisition rather than run more sessions, shrinking the denominator instead of growing the numerator. A good metric needs a paired guardrail — here, subscriber growth — so one number cannot improve by quietly damaging another.

Proxies drift from what they were meant to measure

WCSR proxies for "patients are being helped," not the outcome itself. Coaching practice can change, session length can shrink. A good metric needs periodic re-validation against the real outcome, not a definition trusted forever.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early versus large company

In a consumer product like Ishara Health, with tens of thousands of small, similar accounts, metrics centre on frequency and reach — daily or weekly active users, retention curves — because no single user's behaviour carries much weight. In a B2B product the logic inverts: with perhaps two hundred enterprise accounts, "seats actively using the core feature per account" matters more than any aggregate daily-active number, because losing one large account can outweigh a shift in an average. In a marketplace, a metric on one side is misleading unless paired with its counterpart: a rise in sign-ups would mean little if supply-side capacity could not keep pace — the dilution the worked example surfaced. Stage matters too. An early-stage company, without enough retained cohorts to be statistically meaningful, is often right to track raw behaviour, checked manually. A large company can run tighter, near-real-time metrics, but pays a governance cost: once ten teams build dashboards on one definition, changing it becomes an organisational project.

7. Common mistakes

Vanity inflation. Symptom: leadership cites a number that only ever goes up — total downloads, cumulative registered users — while revenue or retention stalls. Error: conflating reach with value. Diagnostic: would the business act differently if the number doubled overnight? If not, it is a vanity figure, not a metric.

The unowned dashboard tile. Symptom: a number appears in every weekly deck and is discussed in none of the meetings. Error: mistaking measurement for management. Diagnostic: who would lose sleep if the number fell twenty percent next week? Silence is the answer.

The uninstrumented jump. Symptom: a metric moves sharply right after a release with no strategy change behind it. Error: treating an engineering or schema change as neutral. Diagnostic: overlay the metric's timeline against the deployment log before trusting the story anyone tells about it.

The borrowed metric. Symptom: a team adopts a well-known metric — a Net Promoter Score, a "North Star" from a conference talk — because a peer uses it, without checking it fits this business's value exchange. Diagnostic: trace it backward, in one written sentence, to the behaviour it predicts; if that sentence cannot be written, the metric was imported, not built.

8. What good looks like

Two board cycles later, Meher opened with a single slide: WCSR, formula spelled out, owner named as Farah's team, cadence weekly, with the guardrail metric — subscriber growth — beside it so the room could see neither number was being improved at the other's expense. When Rohan asked what would trigger a response if WCSR fell below 0.35, Meher had an answer ready: a review of coach staffing ratios within the week, not a promise to "look into it." The board spent four minutes on the slide instead of the fifteen it had taken to litigate "engagement" in prior quarters. That is the visible signature of a metric that has passed the test: collectable without dispute, quantifiable without ambiguity, tied to a real aspect of performance, and legible as a trend rather than a one-off claim.

9. What Meher decided, and where to go next

Meher retired app opens as Ishara Health's headline number, kept it as an internal signal for the engineering team monitoring app stability, and made WCSR — paired with subscriber growth as a guardrail — the number the board and leadership tracked weekly, with Farah named as owner. The reasoning in her memo followed the four-part test directly: collectable straight from the clinical logging system, quantifiable as an unambiguous rate, tied to the relationship the business actually sold, and comparable week over week against a target and the guardrail.

The natural next question — one Ishara Health had been quietly avoiding — is which of its plausible metrics deserves to be the one number the company rallies around; that is the distinction between vanity and actionable metrics, and the discipline of a single North Star metric, both building on the test worked out here. Two questions are worth sitting with first: if the metric you report most often vanished from your dashboard tomorrow, would anyone act differently for having lost it — and can you name, right now, the one person accountable for making it move?
case20v1-met.what:
Teaching case · What makes a good metric · Sahyog Health

Sahyog Health: The Number in the Contract

1. Opening

At 7.40 on the morning of Thursday, 14 August 2025, Kavitha Ramanathan was in the Sahyog Health office in Hyderabad's Gachibowli, on a call with Singapore and about to join another with New Jersey. In four working days, on 20 August, Sahyog's largest client, Bharosa General Insurance, would sign a three-year renewal worth ₹14.2 crore, and the contract's schedule of service levels had a blank where the "primary engagement metric" should be. Bharosa's procurement team had proposed filling it with monthly active users. Kavitha, Sahyog's head of product, had until Monday to accept that or propose something else, and whatever went into the schedule would determine a performance bonus of up to ₹1.8 crore a year, and also, she suspected, the shape of her roadmap for the next three years.

2. Company background

Sahyog Health was founded in 2019 by two doctors from Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences and a former Practo engineer. It sold a digital diabetes-management programme: an app in which members logged blood glucose, meals and medication, a connected glucometer shipped to their homes, a health coach reachable on WhatsApp, and quarterly HbA1c tests through partner laboratories. It did not sell to individuals. Its customers were insurers, who enrolled policyholders with type 2 diabetes to reduce claims, and large employers, who enrolled staff as a wellness benefit. By mid-2025 it had 96,000 enrolled members across eleven clients, revenue of ₹41 crore in the previous financial year, and 210 staff.

The market was crowded. Fitterfly and HealthifyMe sold comparable programmes, Tata 1mg and Apollo 24|7 bundled diabetes care with pharmacy and diagnostics, and Practo and the insurers' own apps competed for the same screen time. Regulation shaped the product: IRDAI's guidelines on wellness features allowed insurers to offer premium discounts for verified healthy behaviour, which was why insurers cared about engagement at all; the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's health-record standards governed how Sahyog stored lab results; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act constrained what member data could be shared with the insurer. Bharosa, a mid-sized general insurer headquartered in Mumbai with a large group-health book, accounted for 38,000 of Sahyog's members and about a third of its revenue.

3. The situation

Bharosa's request was reasonable on its face. Its group-health actuaries wanted to know whether enrolled members were "using the programme," and monthly active users, defined as members who opened the app at least once in a calendar month, was the number Sahyog had reported in every quarterly review since 2022. It had risen steadily, from 61 percent of enrolled members in early 2024 to 74 percent in July 2025, helped by push notifications, a daily "health tip" screen, and a festival-season steps challenge run around Diwali.

What troubled Kavitha was a piece of work that Neha Kulkarni, Sahyog's data scientist in Toronto, had finished in July. Neha had matched app behaviour to the quarterly HbA1c results for 22,000 Bharosa members with at least two lab tests. Members who logged glucose on twelve or more days a month showed an average HbA1c reduction of 0.9 percentage points over six months, which is clinically meaningful. Members who merely opened the app, without logging, showed essentially no change. The share of members logging twelve or more days had been flat at around 31 percent for a year, while MAU had climbed. The app-opens that drove MAU were, in large part, people tapping a notification and closing the screen.

The global team saw the question from different angles. Daniel Lim, customer-success lead in Singapore, handled Sahyog's Gulf employer clients, including Al Noor Group in Dubai, which enrolled 4,000 of its Indian expatriate staff; Al Noor's HR director had begun asking for "outcomes, not opens" after a rival vendor pitched HbA1c-based pricing. Vikram Rao, sales head in New Jersey, had spent two years building trust with Bharosa's procurement team and did not want the renewal reopened. Lena Fischer, the designer in Berlin, pointed out that the daily health-tip screen, which had lifted MAU more than any other feature, was a screen she had designed to be dismissed in two seconds. The engineers in Hyderabad and Pune noted that MAU was computed from the app analytics event stream, while glucose logs and lab results lived in the clinical database, and that the two had never been reconciled.

4. The people

Kavitha Ramanathan, head of product, Hyderabad. She wants a contract metric that Sahyog can improve by making the programme clinically better, not by making the app noisier, and she wants to sign on time.

Vikram Rao, head of sales, New Jersey. He wants the renewal signed on 20 August with no surprises. His view: "MAU is what they asked for, we are at 74 percent, and the bonus is ours. Don't hand them a number we might miss."

Neha Kulkarni, data scientist, Toronto. She wants the contract to reward the behaviour that actually changes HbA1c, and has the analysis to show which behaviour that is. She is also honest that HbA1c itself is measured only quarterly and only for members who attend the lab test, about 58 percent of them.

Meenakshi Iyer, head of group health at Bharosa, Mumbai. She wants a number her actuaries can put in a model and her board can understand, one that Sahyog cannot inflate, and she has an internal target of a 4 percent reduction in diabetes-related claims cost over the contract term.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Three candidate contract metrics, Bharosa members, July 2025

Candidate metricDefinitionSourceJuly 2025 valueAvailable
Monthly active usersMembers opening the app at least once in the month ÷ enrolled membersApp analytics events74%Monthly, day 2
Engaged loggersMembers logging glucose on 12 or more days in the month ÷ enrolled membersClinical database31%Monthly, day 2
HbA1c respondersMembers with a 0.5-point or greater reduction at six months ÷ members with two testsPartner lab results46%Quarterly, 6-month lag; 58% of members tested

Enrolled Bharosa members: 38,000. Bonus in Bharosa's draft schedule: ₹60 lakh per year for each of three tiers reached on the primary metric, up to ₹1.8 crore. Source: company data, Neha Kulkarni's July analysis.

Exhibit 1 sets the three numbers side by side. MAU is the highest and the easiest to collect, but it comes from the event stream, which the engineers had not reconciled with the clinical records. Engaged loggers is lower, and collected from the system of record; every glucose reading is a row in the clinical database and cannot be created by a notification. HbA1c responders is the number Meenakshi's actuaries ultimately care about, but it arrives with a six-month lag and covers only the members who go for the lab test.

Exhibit 2. MAU and engaged loggers, Bharosa members, August 2024 to July 2025

MAU from app analytics; engaged loggers from clinical database. The Diwali challenge in late October 2024 lifted MAU by 3 points for one month with no visible effect on logging.

Exhibit 2 is the picture that had kept Kavitha awake. Over twelve months the two lines had come apart: the number Sahyog reported went up, and the number that predicted health outcomes did not move. If the contract paid on MAU, every incentive on her roadmap would push the top line further from the bottom one.

Exhibit 3. Six-month HbA1c change by monthly logging band, 22,000 Bharosa members with two tests

Logging days per monthMembersShare of testedMean HbA1c change (points)Responders (≥0.5 reduction)
0 to 3 (opens only, or nothing)9,24042%−0.128%
4 to 115,72026%−0.445%
12 or more7,04032%−0.971%

Observational, not a randomised comparison; members who log more may differ in motivation. Bharosa estimates each 0.5-point HbA1c reduction sustained for a year saves about ₹4,200 in claims per member. Source: Neha Kulkarni, July 2025.

Exhibit 3 is the evidence that connects behaviour to outcome. The gradient is steep: members in the top logging band were two and a half times as likely to be responders as those who merely opened the app. Neha was careful to note that the comparison was observational, and that the 42 percent of tested members in the lowest band were not a random sample of the enrolled population. Even so, the footnote's claims-saving figure let Kavitha do a rough sum. If Sahyog could move 5,000 members from the lowest band to the highest, at roughly 0.8 points of additional reduction each, the implied claims saving to Bharosa was in the region of ₹3.4 crore a year, which was more than the entire bonus pool.

6. The options

Option A: Accept monthly active users. Sign on 20 August with the metric Bharosa proposed. The upside is certainty: the renewal closes, the bonus tiers are set at 70, 75 and 80 percent, and Sahyog is already at 74. The cost is that the contract would reward the least meaningful behaviour, that the roadmap would tilt towards notifications and dismissible screens, and that Al Noor and other outcome-minded clients would see Sahyog pricing itself on opens while rivals priced on results. There was also an unexamined risk in the number itself: MAU came from an event stream nobody had reconciled.

Option B: Propose engaged loggers as the primary metric, with HbA1c responders reported alongside. Replace MAU with the share of members logging glucose on twelve or more days a month, set tiers at 33, 38 and 43 percent, and commit to reporting HbA1c responder rate quarterly as an information item rather than a bonus condition. The upside is that the bonus would pay for the behaviour that Exhibit 3 shows changes outcomes, the number is collectable monthly from the system of record, and it gives Meenakshi's actuaries something they can model. The costs are that Sahyog starts at 31 percent, below the first tier, that reopening the schedule four days before signing tests Vikram's relationship, and that Bharosa may ask why Sahyog had been reporting MAU for three years.

Option C: Propose HbA1c responders as the primary metric. Put the clinical outcome directly into the contract, with tiers at 45, 50 and 55 percent. The upside is alignment: it is exactly what Bharosa is paying for, and it would be the strongest possible pitch to Al Noor. The costs are structural. The number is available only quarterly with a six-month lag, so Sahyog would not know for nine months whether it was on track; it covers only the 58 percent of members who go for testing, so it could be moved by encouraging the healthiest members to test; and Sahyog does not control the lab network's turnaround or the members' attendance.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Test each of the three candidate numbers in Exhibit 1 against the four properties of a good metric: collectable, quantifiable, tracking an aspect of performance, and over time. Which properties does each pass, and which does it fail?

2. Exhibit 2 shows MAU rising while engaged loggers stayed flat. What does this divergence tell you about what MAU was actually measuring? What would you want the engineers to check before Sahyog reports MAU again?

3. If the contract pays on engaged loggers, what is the easiest way for Sahyog to move the number without improving anyone's health, and what guardrail would you add to the schedule to catch it?

4. Which option should Kavitha take by Monday, and how should she present it to Vikram in New Jersey and Meenakshi in Mumbai so that neither feels the renewal is at risk?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single idea: a metric is a number that is collectable the same way every period, quantifiable by a defined formula, tracks an aspect of performance, and can be compared over time. Bharosa's proposed number passes the first, second and fourth tests easily, which is why it was proposed. It fails the third. Exhibit 2 is the evidence: MAU rose for a year while the behaviour that predicts outcomes did not, so MAU was tracking Sahyog's notification strategy, not the programme's performance.

A well-reasoned answer works through all three candidates rather than jumping to the one that sounds most virtuous. HbA1c responders tracks performance best but fails on collectability and timeliness: a number that arrives nine months late, for half the population, cannot steer a monthly programme, and can be gamed by who gets tested. Engaged loggers sits between the two. It is collected monthly from the clinical database, which is the system of record; it cannot be inflated by a push notification; and Exhibit 3 gives a credible link from it to the outcome the client is paying for.

One defensible path is Option B, with three additions that address its costs. First, propose the change to Meenakshi with Exhibits 2 and 3 in hand, framed as Sahyog volunteering a stricter number, which converts a late reopening into a demonstration of good faith and gives her actuaries the model-ready input they want. Second, add a guardrail to the schedule: the share of tested members must not fall below 55 percent, so that Sahyog cannot hit the logging tiers while letting lab attendance drift. Third, commit to reporting HbA1c responders every quarter as an information item, so that if the link between logging and outcomes weakens, both parties see it. Vikram's concern is real, and the answer to it is that a contract paying ₹1.8 crore a year on a number Sahyog knows to be hollow is a larger risk to the relationship than a candid conversation four days before signing.

The general lesson is that every metric in a contract, a dashboard or a quarterly review should have an owner, a cadence and a decision it informs, and that the third of these is the test most numbers fail. Learners who want to go further should look next at vanity versus actionable metrics, and then at the North Star metric, which asks what single number a company like Sahyog should steer by across all its clients.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement · Deep reading

What Makes a Good Metric

Two product leaders, one in freight and one in enterprise learning, find in the same fortnight that their headline numbers are honest, well instrumented, widely trusted — and wrong in ways that cost money.

1. Two rooms, two numbers

Gurugram, 6 February 2026. Aparna Ravikumar, vice-president of product at Qaafila Freight Exchange, was preparing the data room for a Series C. Qaafila matched shippers with truck owners on the Delhi–Mumbai and Nagpur–Bengaluru corridors: about one lakh loads posted a week, ₹4,200 crore of annualised booking value, 12,000 active shippers. For eighteen months the headline number had been loads posted per week, up 41 per cent year on year, and never questioned.

It was questioned by Vikrant Ahuja, who ran corridor operations from Nagpur. His fleet partners said Qaafila had stopped showing them the difficult loads — over-dimensional consignments, return legs out of Guwahati. Match rate, the share of posted loads finding a confirmed truck within six hours, had risen from 62 to 68 per cent over the quarter. The ops team's incentive was paid on match rate. The number of loads that moved had fallen.

Pune, 11 February 2026. Zoya Mirza, director of product at Prerana Learning Systems, was five days from a renewal forecast review. Prerana sold compliance and skills training to large Indian employers: 214 accounts, 4.8 lakh licensed seats, ₹310 crore of recurring revenue. Her dashboard said average seat activation was 47 per cent and rising. Anirban Sen, who led customer success from Kolkata, said the accounts he worried about all sat near 30 per cent — three of them, worth ₹41 crore, renewing inside ninety days.

Neither number was fabricated. Both were collectable, quantifiable, plainly about performance and tracked over time — the four properties separating a metric from a passing observation. That test is necessary but not sufficient, and this page concerns the second set experts apply underneath it: sensitivity, correct unit of analysis, resistance to the incentive it sits inside, and a validated link to the outcome the business sells.

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

A metric is a number an organisation deliberately collects in a repeatable way, expresses in comparable units, and tracks over time because it stands in for an aspect of performance. The definition is easy. The craft lies in the operational definition, which has six slots most teams fill implicitly and argue about later: the population covered, the event that counts, the window, the unit of analysis, the unit of aggregation, and the system of record. Qaafila's match rate had all six unstated: "matched" meant a carrier tap rather than a confirmed pickup, and the window was undefined on Sundays.

The intellectual history is older than software. V. F. Ridgway's 1956 paper on the dysfunctional consequences of performance measurement catalogued, with factory evidence, how single measures distort behaviour. Goodhart's 1975 remark on monetary targets and Campbell's 1976 law generalised it: a measure used for control ceases to be a good measure. Eccles's performance-measurement manifesto (1991) and Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard (1992) answered with breadth rather than scepticism. The product literature arrived later — Kaushik separating interesting numbers from actionable ones; Croll and Yoskovitz proposing in Lean Analytics (2013) that a good metric is comparative, understandable and usually a rate; Kohavi, Tang and Xu's Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020) bringing the overall evaluation criterion into product practice; Muller's The Tyranny of Metrics (2018) restating the sceptical case.

Five positions survive, and they genuinely conflict.

Table 1 — A practitioner who cannot state these is borrowing one camp's answer without knowing it.
CampWill signWill not sign
Actionable-metrics (Kaushik, Croll & Yoskovitz)A number that cannot change a decision this quarter should goThat one number should steer a company for years
North Star / metrics-tree (Ellis lineage, Amplitude, Reforge)One output metric encoding the value exchange, decomposed into inputs teams ownThat each team picks whatever is locally actionable
Experimentation (Kohavi, Tang, Xu)A metric unable to detect real change in two weeks is not decision-gradeThat understandable and actionable suffices
Control / scorecard (Drucker, Kaplan & Norton, Eccles)No single measure; a balanced set with financial counterweightsOne metric that matters, in any form
Sceptics (Ridgway, Goodhart, Campbell, Muller)Any measure tied to reward will be gamed; diagnose, do not steerThat better design outruns the incentive problem

Aparna's problem is the sceptics' case made concrete; Zoya's is the experimentation camp's, since at 214 accounts nothing measured weekly carries enough signal to settle an argument.

3. Mechanics in depth: the eight steps, four of them usually implicit

Expert practice runs a fixed sequence. Write the operational definition across its six slots. Choose the unit of analysis and check it against the unit of randomisation. Measure variance before using the level. Compute sensitivity — the smallest change you could detect. Attack it: name the cheapest way to move it ten per cent without helping a customer. Pair it with guardrails. Validate the proxy against a long-horizon outcome. Only then assign owner, cadence and decision rule. The four middle steps are the ones teams skip, and where both protagonists went wrong.

Sensitivity, worked

Sriram Balaji, Qaafila's data science lead in Chennai, ran the arithmetic that should have been run eighteen months earlier. For a two-arm test at 80 per cent power and five per cent significance, the minimum detectable effect is approximately

MDE ≈ 2.8 × σ × √(2 / n)    and in relative terms    MDE% ≈ 2.8 × CV × √(2 / n)

where 2.8 is the sum of the two critical values (1.96 + 0.84), n is the sample per arm, and CV is the standard deviation over the mean. With 12,000 shippers per arm, √(2/12,000) = 0.0129. Loads posted per shipper had mean 3.4 and standard deviation 9.1 — CV 2.68 — so its relative MDE was 2.8 × 2.68 × 0.0129 = 9.7 per cent. Match rate per shipper had mean 0.62 and standard deviation 0.21, CV 0.34, giving 1.2 per cent: eight times more sensitive on the same traffic. Qaafila had spent eighteen months experimenting against the least sensitive number in the building and calling most results inconclusive.

The unit of analysis, and the correction nobody remembers

Qaafila randomised by shipper but analysed by load, because loads were what the pipeline emitted. Each shipper posted 8.7 loads a week, and loads from one shipper resembled each other: intra-shipper correlation 0.31. The design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 7.7 × 0.31 = 3.39, so the honest standard error is 1.84 times the naive one. A result from the previous quarter with a naive z of 2.4 — a confident p of 0.016 — became z = 1.30, p = 0.19. The feature had shipped. The definition was not wrong; the arithmetic underneath the comparison was.

Variance before level

Know a metric's weekly noise before reacting to its weekly moves. Qaafila's match rate had a standard deviation of 0.9 percentage points across 26 weeks, once corridor seasonality was removed: a 0.6-point move was noise and should never have reached a leadership agenda. There is a multiplicity trap alongside it — a dashboard of forty tiles flagged at two standard deviations lights up about two tiles a week by chance. The competent practitioner investigates them; the expert asks how many tiles are on the board.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, stated as testable claims. C1: a repeatable system of record exists. True at Qaafila, where every posting and confirmation is a row, corroborated by e-way bill and FASTag trails. Partly true at Prerana, whose platform logs completions but whose seat entitlements live in each customer's identity system. C2: the behaviour recurs often enough that a reporting period carries signal. True at Qaafila; false at Prerana account-level, since 214 accounts renewing annually is 214 observations a year — a qualitative problem wearing a dashboard's clothes. C3: the denominator is stable and meaningful. False at Qaafila once ops could influence what got posted. C4: the link to value is validated, not assumed. Neither company had tested it.

Where the apparatus actively misleads: before product-market fit, when a metric freezes a guess about the behaviour worth wanting; for one-shot decisions such as pricing architecture, where there is no series to trend; and in novel categories, where available proxies measure the old behaviour well and the new one not at all.

5. Hard edges: two-sided, multi-product, regulated, hardware, AI

In a two-sided market, any single-side metric is a half-truth. Qaafila's supply lead in Ludhiana, Harleen Kaur Sethi, tracked truck utilisation; Aparna tracked shipper posting. A marketplace's honest metric is a match metric with both sides' counts beside it, since liquidity improves by shrinking either side. In multi-product companies the seam is definitional: Pankti Retail, selling a kirana point-of-sale system and a credit line, counted 96,000 active merchants in one P&L and 71,000 in the other.

Regulated products lose the freedom to define. Rekha Credit, a Mumbai non-banking financial company, cannot invent a convenient definition of a current account: days-past-due buckets and the ninety-day non-performing-asset rule are set by the Reserve Bank of India, and its collection-efficiency metric must reconcile to that series or the gap becomes an audit finding. The DPDP Act, 2023 adds a second constraint: unconsented telemetry is not awkward, it is unavailable.

Hardware compounds the denominator problem. Roshni Power Devices had shipped 2.4 lakh solar inverters, but only 71 per cent were connected and nine per cent sat in distributor warehouses past ninety days. Every rate Roshni reported hid an unknown 29 per cent, and its installed-base denominator led reality by a quarter. AI-native products break the series differently: when Qalam AI swapped its model, output distributions shifted and the old metric kept its name while ceasing to mean what it had meant. Only an eval suite held fixed across the change could say whether quality improved.

At the organisational seam, what mature companies do rarely matches what they describe. The stated practice is a governed metric layer; the observed practice is perhaps fifteen certified, versioned metrics with a changelog and a steward, surrounded by hundreds of uncertified numbers teams actually run on. The discipline is not to abolish the long tail but to insist that anything reaching a board slide or a compensation plan comes from the certified set.

6. Nine things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Sensitivity, not elegance, decides which metric you can actually use

The tell is a team whose experiments keep returning inconclusive while decisions get made on intuition. The obvious reading blames weak ideas; the usual truth is a high-variance metric — a fat-tailed count, or revenue dominated by a few accounts. Experts check the coefficient of variation before the roadmap.

The unit of analysis is a design decision, not a pipeline detail

The tell is a per-event average quoted in a discussion about users. Per-event and per-user means diverge whenever usage is skewed, and heavy users write the headline. Qaafila's load-level average described its fifty largest shippers; its shipper-level average described the market.

Every ratio is two stories, and reporting one is a choice

The tell is a rate presented without its numerator and denominator. A rate improves because the good thing grew or the base shrank, and the second is easier. Experts write rates as triples and treat components moving in opposite directions as the finding, not the footnote.

Every metric has an implied population, and it is usually survivors

The tell is an activation number improving steadily in a quarter when churn was high: accounts that left stopped contributing observations, so the average rose because the unhappy exited the denominator. The diagnostic is to recompute on the opening cohort.

A metric's variance is itself a metric worth knowing

The tell is someone quoting the weekly standard deviation before the level. Without it, reviews become stories told about noise, and numbers mean whatever the most confident person in the room says.

Proxies decay, and almost nobody schedules the revalidation

The tell is a metric whose correlation with the real outcome was measured once, at adoption, then cited for years. Products change and the behaviour the proxy stood for moves out from under it. Experts put a revalidation date in the definition and treat a fallen correlation as grounds for retirement.

Gameability is a property of the incentive, not of the number

The tell is a metric that began behaving strangely in the quarter someone's variable pay was attached to it. No definitional cleverness survives a compensation plan; Ridgway and Goodhart described incentives, not arithmetic. The diagnostic is who is paid on this, and what the cheapest path to the bonus is.

A definition change is a silent regime change

The tell is a step in a series lining up with a deployment date rather than a market event: comparing across it compares two measurements wearing one name. Experts version definitions, backfill where they can, and mark the break when they cannot.

Segment before you aggregate; mix shift is the commonest false alarm

The tell is an aggregate falling while every segment rises, or the reverse — Simpson's paradox, not a curiosity but the ordinary consequence of a growing company changing its own mix. The obvious reading, that the product got worse, is wrong often enough that the segment view should be the default.

7. How this differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products the numbers are large, the behaviour frequent, experimentation the primary instrument; the hard problems are novelty effects and gaming. In B2B and enterprise, small n governs: Prerana cannot experiment its way to an answer about 214 accounts, so it combines weighted aggregates, leading indicators and structured conversation. In marketplaces, metrics come in pairs and the match metric outranks either side. In hardware, denominators lag physical reality and telemetry coverage is a metric about the metrics. In AI products, evaluation suites take the place instrumented behaviour occupies elsewhere, because no logged event says whether the output was good.

What does not differ is worth saying plainly: the six-slot definition, owner, cadence and decision rule are identical across all of these. By stage the difference is narrower than folklore suggests. Early companies should track fewer, blunter numbers read alongside conversations, lacking volume for sensitivity anyway. Growth-stage companies need guardrails, because this is when incentives first get attached. At scale the constraint is governance: once forty teams build on one definition, changing it costs months — which is why large companies keep bad metrics long after they know better.

8. Three worked examples

Prerana: the same data, two defensible averages

Deepa Krishnan, Prerana's analytics lead in Coimbatore, reconstructed both numbers. Seat-weighted activation — active learners over licensed seats — was 38.0 per cent. The unweighted mean of each account's rate was 47.0 per cent. Both were correct. The gap was structural: 18 large accounts held 3.0 of the 4.8 lakh seats. They also held 71 per cent of ARR while activating at 31 per cent, while 196 mid-sized accounts activated at about 48.5 per cent apiece and dominated an unweighted average.

Table 2 — Prerana Learning Systems; seats in lakh. Both segments improve; the aggregate does not, because the seat mix moved toward the harder segment.

Seat-weighted total4.8038.0%5.6037.9%

The next quarter Prerana signed 80,000 new large-account seats, which activate slowly. Large-account activation rose a point to 32 per cent and mid-account activation eight tenths of a point, yet the seat-weighted total fell from 38.0 to 37.9 per cent, because the share of seats in the harder segment rose from 62 to 68 per cent. An executive reading the aggregate would conclude the product had deteriorated; one reading the account mean, up to 47.9, would conclude all was well. Both would be reading a mix shift. Zoya made the segmented view the default and defined renewal risk on the ARR-weighted number, the currency the company loses.

Qaafila: a rate improved by removing the difficult work

Sriram reconstructed the quarter's arithmetic on a base of 1,00,000 posted loads a week.

Table 3 — Qaafila, weekly steady state. The metric that paid the bonus improved 6.4 points while the business it stood for shrank.

They had rationally stopped soliciting the twelve thousand weekly postings least likely to match — over-dimensional cargo, monsoon north-east return legs — of which about fifteen per cent would have found a truck. Match rate rose 6.4 points; 1,800 fewer loads moved weekly; repeat posting fell five points as shippers learned the platform was not for their hard freight. The recovery had three parts: the incentive moved onto matched loads with a rate floor; posted loads per shipper became a mandatory guardrail on the same slide; and match rate was stratified, the hard-load segment given its own floor, so improving an average by abandoning a segment became visible.

Qalam AI: where the approach failed outright

Qalam AI, a Hyderabad company selling an AI drafting assistant to law firms and insurers, had chosen suggestion acceptance rate as its quality metric — defensible, instrumented, sensitive. Tanmay Deshpande's team shipped a change making suggestions shorter and safer. Acceptance rose from 22 to 31 per cent. But with twelve suggestions in a typical session and mean accepted length falling from 41 to 19 characters, characters accepted per session fell from 108 to 71 — a 35 per cent decline in work done for the user. Sixty-day retention fell from 48 to 41 per cent across two cohorts.

The metric passed every test the team knew and failed the one they did not: its link to value had never been validated. Across forty weekly cohorts, acceptance rate correlated with sixty-day retention at r = 0.08. The replacement — accepted characters surviving unedited 24 hours later, per active session — correlated at 0.61, gated by a fixed suite of 300 graded prompts run on every model change so a swap could not quietly redefine quality. Recovery took two quarters; the expensive part was the roadmap built on the old metric.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Denominator gaming. Early sign: a rate improving while its numerator is flat or falling. Diagnostic: plot numerator and denominator together for six months. Caught late, a segment has been quietly taught that the product is not for them — expensive to win back, invisible in the metric that caused it.

The insensitive headline. Early sign: inconclusive experiments and rising reliance on opinion. Diagnostic: compute the coefficient of variation and implied MDE at current traffic. Caught late, a company spends a year unable to tell good work from bad.

Mix-shift misreading. Early sign: aggregate and segments disagreeing in direction. Diagnostic: hold the mix at prior-period weights. Caught late, teams are reorganised to fix a problem that never existed.

Unvalidated proxy. Early sign: nobody can say when the link to retention or revenue was last measured. Diagnostic: ask for the correlation and its date. Caught late, a roadmap optimises something customers do not value.

Silent redefinition. Early sign: a step change matching a release date. Diagnostic: overlay the deployment log. Caught late, a board is shown an artefact, and the credibility cost lands on the product team.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One metric that matters, or a balanced set? The single-metric camp argues from organisational physics: a company holds one number in its head, and a scorecard of twelve becomes a scorecard of none. The scorecard camp argues from Ridgway: every single measure has an exposed flank, and a company steered by one number finds it at scale. For the first to be wrong you would have to show organisations reliably attending to several numbers at once; for the second, a single metric surviving a decade of incentive pressure undistorted. Neither has been shown.

Sensitivity or interpretability? The experimentation camp accepts a composite, variance-reduced metric no executive can explain, because it decides questions the interpretable one cannot. The business camp answers that an unexplainable metric cannot be argued with, therefore cannot be owned, and becomes a number the data team asserts. The evidence is split: large experimentation programmes resolve far more decisions with engineered metrics, while smaller organisations that adopt them often stop discussing them at all.

Should metrics carry targets? The accountability position holds that a metric without a target is a report, and reports do not change behaviour. The Goodhart position holds that once a target is set, especially one tied to pay, the metric measures compliance rather than reality — exactly what Qaafila observed. A middle neither camp fully endorses: targets on outcomes, floors on guardrails, never bonuses on ratios.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic recites that a metric should be collectable, quantifiable, performance-linked and tracked over time, and produces a clean dashboard. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They ask what the denominator is before what the number is. They know their metrics' weekly noise by heart and decline to discuss moves inside it. For any metric they own, they can state the cheapest dishonest way to improve it and the guardrail that catches it. And they retire metrics — the rarest behaviour, because killing one costs more political capital than adding ten.

12. What each protagonist decided

Aparna took matched loads per active shipper to the board, not match rate, with posted loads per shipper as a published guardrail and the hard-load segment reported against its own floor. She moved the ops incentive off the ratio, which cost her a month with the chief executive, Devang Shroff, who had liked the rising rate. Her argument was Table 3: the company had been paying people to shrink itself.

Zoya did something less dramatic and arguably harder. She demoted the aggregate, made the segmented ARR-weighted view the default, and wrote a one-page operational definition with all six slots filled, a steward in Anirban's team, a weekly cadence and a decision rule: any account below 25 per cent activation ninety days before renewal triggers an executive review. She also commissioned the validation nobody had run — whether seat activation predicts renewal at all.

Three questions. First: had Qaafila's ops incentive never existed, would match rate have been a good metric — or does a metric's quality depend on the organisation it sits inside? Second: Prerana's two averages were both correct; on what principle should a company choose, and who owns that choice? Third: Qalam's acceptance rate was sensitive, cheap and honest, and it cost two quarters. What test, applied before adoption, would have caught it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Vanity vs actionable metrics — the sharpest filter for numbers that survive a board slide but change nothing.
  2. GAME framework — deriving goals, actions, metrics and evaluation instead of inheriting a dashboard.
  3. North Star metric — how one company-level output metric is chosen, and what breaks when it is not.
  4. UX metrics (HEART) — a vocabulary for measuring experience quality where behavioural counts say nothing.
  5. Writing an experiment hypothesis — turning a good metric into a decision you can defend.
  6. What evals are and why PMs own them — the AI-native successor to instrumentation.
  7. Analytics when anyone can query the data — governance after self-service removes the gatekeeper.
  8. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — where in the lifecycle a metric belongs.
  9. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — the vocabulary for choices made throughout this page.
  10. Attention, transaction, productivity games — which metrics are native to the game your product plays.
  11. Breadth × depth × frequency — decomposing engagement into three factors teams can separately own.
  12. Input vs output; leading vs lagging — why guardrails and early-warning metrics differ in kind.
  13. One Metric That Matters — the strongest single-metric case and when it holds.

Teaching case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Kahani Audio

Kahani Audio: Eleven Million Hours

1. The night before

At 11.20 p.m. on Sunday, 13 September 2026, Devika Sharma was still at the dining table of her flat in Gurugram's Sector 54, with a laptop, a printed board deck, and a WhatsApp thread with Toronto that had been active since her afternoon. She was chief product officer of Kahani Audio, a vernacular audio-stories app with 14 million monthly listeners, and at 10 a.m. the next morning the board would meet to approve the metric on which the company's next twelve months, its Series C data room, and a founder equity tranche worth roughly ₹38 crore would all turn.

The deck said that Kahani's listeners had consumed 11.2 million hours of audio a day in August, a figure that had grown 71 percent in a year and had been the first line of every investor update since 2023. The WhatsApp thread said that somewhere between 14 and 31 percent of those hours had probably not been heard by anyone, and that nobody could yet say which end of that range was right. Devika had to decide, before the board did, whether to present the 11.2 million, to present a corrected number she could not fully defend, or to propose that the company stop steering by hours altogether. Each choice had a cost that landed on a different person in a different city.

2. Company history

Kahani Audio was founded in Gurugram in 2020 by Manav Chopra, a former Jio content executive, and Rohit Bansal, an engineer from Paytm. Its bet was that India's next hundred million internet users would want long-form serialised stories in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Marathi, read aloud, and that they would listen the way an earlier generation had followed television serials: an episode a night, for months. By 2026 it had 2.1 lakh episodes across 3,400 series, produced by a network of freelance writers and voice artists paid per episode, and it competed directly with Pocket FM and Kuku FM, and less directly with Spotify, JioSaavn and YouTube.

The company made money three ways. About 6.8 lakh listeners paid a subscription, ₹99 to ₹399 a month, collected through UPI autopay, Google Play billing and, in the Gulf, carrier billing. Advertising, sold mainly to consumer brands wanting Hindi-speaking audiences and, through a New Jersey office, to American brands targeting the diaspora, produced about 40 percent of revenue. And a bundling deal with a Gulf telecom operator, Al Madar Telecom, delivered Kahani to 9 lakh Indian expatriate subscribers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar for a per-subscriber fee. Revenue in the year to March 2026 was ₹212 crore, with an operating loss of ₹64 crore.

The decision that constrained everything now had been taken in the Series B, in November 2023. Peepal Ventures, a Mumbai growth fund, had led a ₹340 crore round on the condition that the company adopt a single key performance indicator against which management would be measured. Daily listening hours was chosen, over daily active listeners, because Manav argued that hours captured depth of engagement and were harder to inflate with notifications. The term sheet attached a founder equity tranche to it: 2.4 percent of the company would vest to Manav and Rohit if daily listening hours exceeded 12 million by 31 March 2027, as measured by "the company's standard reporting." Nobody in that room had asked what the company's standard reporting counted, or what would happen if the way it counted changed.

3. The industry

Indian audio streaming in 2026 was a crowded and unevenly monetised market. Pocket FM and Kuku FM had both raised large rounds and pushed hard into micro-payments and international markets; Spotify and JioSaavn dominated music; YouTube was the largest audio platform in the country by any measure and charged nothing. Listening time was the industry's public currency, quoted in press releases and pitch decks, partly because it was the number advertisers understood, and partly because subscription numbers were small and lumpy.

Three regulatory and platform forces bore on Kahani. The Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework for recurring payments required additional authentication for autopay above certain limits and had, since 2021, produced a steady leak of failed renewals across every subscription business in the country; Kahani's own renewal failure rate on UPI autopay ran at 9 to 12 percent a month. Google Play's billing policies governed what share of in-app subscription revenue Kahani kept and how it could steer users to cheaper payment routes. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, with rules notified in 2025, constrained what listening data could be shared with advertisers and partners, which mattered because Kahani's American advertisers and its Gulf telecom partner both wanted more granular listening data than the company was now comfortable providing.

The global exposure cut two ways. The Al Madar bundle in the Gulf was the company's most profitable line, with almost no acquisition cost, but the contract came up for renewal in December 2026 and Al Madar's commercial team wanted to move from a per-subscriber fee to a per-hour fee, which would make Kahani's listening-hours definition a matter of contract rather than convention. In New Jersey, the ad-sales team sold "listener hours" as inventory to brands whose media agencies were, in 2026, increasingly asking for third-party measurement.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence began in February 2025, when Tobias Weber's design team in Berlin shipped an autoplay feature: when an episode ended, the next one started after a five-second countdown. It was tested for ten days on 8 percent of Android users. Listening hours per listener rose 18 percent; episode completion rate fell 11 percent; thirty-day retention rose two points, which the data team flagged as not statistically significant; paid conversion was flat. The test overlapped the first week of the IPL cricket season, when evening listening dipped for everyone. Management read the result as a clear win on the KPI and rolled autoplay out to all users in March. At that point it was believed that hours were a good proxy for listener value, and the completion-rate decline was explained as a consequence of listeners sampling more series.

In October 2025 the Bengaluru engineering team released background playback on Android, so that stories continued when the phone was locked or the app was minimised. Hours rose again. What was believed at the time was that background playback had unlocked commuting and household listening, which was consistent with the company's picture of its audience: women in tier-2 cities listening while cooking, men listening on two-wheelers with one earphone. Kahani's "hours" number came from the client: the app fired a heartbeat event every thirty seconds of playback, and the analytics pipeline summed them.

In August 2026, Aisha Rahman, head of data in Toronto, was building a server-side measure of hours from the content-delivery logs, for the Al Madar negotiation, and found that server-side hours were about 22 percent lower than client-side hours in August, and that the gap had opened in October 2025. Three explanations were on the table, and they were not exclusive. First, background playback on some Android builds kept sending heartbeats after the audio session had been silenced by the operating system, so hours were being counted while nothing played. Second, autoplay meant that episodes ran on after a listener had put the phone down or fallen asleep, so hours were played but not heard. Third, the server-side logs were themselves incomplete: iOS delivery went through a different CDN whose logs had not been ingested for a five-week period, and Gulf traffic was partly served from Al Madar's own caches. The 14-to-31 percent range in Devika's WhatsApp thread was the spread between the most and least generous ways of reconciling these.

What had since turned out to be wrong was more than the number. The February 2025 test had been read as evidence that autoplay improved engagement; it now looked at least as consistent with autoplay improving the count of hours while making each hour less meaningful. The retention gain had been non-significant and the completion decline had been real. And the assumption in the Series B that hours were "harder to inflate" had been correct about notifications and wrong about product design.

5. The people

Devika Sharma, chief product officer, Gurugram. Joined in 2024 from Zomato. Her position is that the company should steer by a metric that counts listeners, not hours, and she has a candidate: weekly listeners who complete at least three episodes. Her incentive is a CPO's: a metric she can move with product quality rather than autoplay timers. What she is not saying is that the candidate metric has fallen 4 percent in six months, which is not the story a data room wants.

Manav Chopra, co-founder and chief executive, Gurugram. His position is that the hours number must be corrected but not abandoned, because "investors have three years of it and we cannot walk into a Series C with a new yardstick." His incentive is the equity tranche, which at the last round's valuation is worth about ₹38 crore to him and Rohit; he says this openly. What he is not saying is that he spoke to Peepal's partner informally in July, before the gap was found, about whether the March 2027 threshold might be revisited, and was told no.

Sunil Krishnan, partner, Peepal Ventures, Mumbai, board member. His position is that the KPI is a contractual matter and that any restatement must be documented and audited before the board adopts it. His incentive is a fund with a mark on Kahani that depends on a clean Series C. What he is not saying is that Peepal's own limited partners have seen the 11.2 million figure in the fund's quarterly letter.

Aisha Rahman, head of data, Toronto. Her position is that neither number, client or server, is currently a metric; both are estimates with unknown error, and the company should say so. Her incentive is professional: she does not want to sign off on a restated figure that is later shown to be wrong. What she is not saying is that she believes the heartbeat problem was noticed by an engineer in December 2025, who left the company in February, and that a ticket exists.

Tobias Weber, head of design, Berlin. His position is that autoplay is standard across every streaming product in the world and that removing it to make a number look honest would be self-harm. His incentive is a feature he championed. What he is not saying is that his own team's qualitative research in June, twelve interviews in Lucknow and Coimbatore, found that seven listeners described waking up to a story they had not chosen, and two had uninstalled the app over it.

Priyanka Menon, head of advertising sales, New Jersey. Her position is that any public correction to hours would be used by agencies to demand make-goods on campaigns already delivered, potentially ₹6 to 9 crore. Her incentive is a sales target set on the old inventory number. What she is not saying is that one agency has already asked, in writing, for a third-party audit of Kahani's listening data before renewing a ₹4.5 crore annual commitment.

Farhan Qureshi, regional director for the Gulf, Dubai. His position is that the Al Madar renewal should stay on a per-subscriber fee and that Kahani should not volunteer hours data into the negotiation. His incentive is a renewal bonus. What he is not saying is that Al Madar's commercial team has its own server-side listening data from its caches and has hinted that it does not match Kahani's.

Kavya Nair, engineering lead, Bengaluru. Her position is that the heartbeat fix is written and can ship in the next Android release on 22 September, after which client-side hours will fall by an amount she estimates at 12 to 15 percent. What she is not saying is that iOS has a smaller version of the same problem that has not been investigated, because the team was told the deadline was Monday.

Worse, the footnote revealed that the control group had been contaminated by the rollout before its thirty-day retention could be read, so even the non-significant retention gain was not clean. What the exhibit did show, unambiguously, was that the one metric the company steered by had been moved by a feature whose effect on every other measure was flat or negative.

8. The options as Devika currently sees them

Keep hours, correct quietly. Present the 11.2 million on Monday with a footnote that an instrumentation review is under way, ship Kavya's fix on the 22nd, and restate the series in the October board pack once the corrected number is known. This kept the Series C narrative intact and gave the team three weeks to understand the error. It also meant the board would approve a plan, and the data room would open, on a number the company's own head of data had said in writing was not reliable; and if Al Madar or Omnicom raised the gap first, the October restatement would look like a response rather than a disclosure.

Switch the KPI to listeners. Propose weekly listeners completing three or more episodes as the company's metric, present Exhibit 6, and ask the board to treat the hours series as a legacy figure for advertising inventory only. This was the option Devika believed in, and it had the defect that the new metric was six days old, fell over the year, came from the same fault-prone event stream, and would put the tranche clause into immediate dispute, because the clause named hours and the company would be saying hours no longer measured what it had been chosen to measure.

Report both and defer the decision. Take Sunil's suggestion: adopt nothing, present both series with their footnotes, commission an external review, and return in October. This was defensible and slow. The data room was due to open on 1 October with or without a decision; the Al Madar renewal talks began in November; Priyanka's agency wanted an answer within the month; and Manav's view was that a board that adopted nothing was a board that had lost confidence in its own numbers, which would be visible to the Series C investors in the minutes.

What Devika had begun to suspect, late on Sunday, was that the three options shared an assumption she had not examined: that the company needed one number, that the number should be chosen on Monday, and that choosing it was her decision to bring. It was possible that the real question was not which metric but who owned the definition, or whether the tranche clause could be separated from the operating metric, or whether a company selling hours to advertisers and subscribers to Al Madar and stories to listeners should expect any single number to serve all three. It was also possible that this was the kind of thought a chief product officer had at 11.20 p.m. to avoid choosing.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board would meet at 10 a.m. on Monday, 14 September 2026, for two hours, with Sunil on video from Mumbai and an independent director from Bengaluru in the room. The Series C data room opened on 1 October and the bankers had asked for three years of consistent KPI history. The founder tranche, 2.4 percent of the company, vested on 12 million daily hours by 31 March 2027 "as measured by the company's standard reporting," and the August figure was 11.2 million client-side or roughly 8.7 million by Aisha's reconstruction. Kahani had ₹118 crore of cash, about fourteen months at the current burn, and no committed Series C lead. The advertising contracts delivered against listener-hours contained make-good clauses, and one renewal worth ₹4.5 crore was contingent on an audit the company had not yet agreed to. The Al Madar contract, ₹36 crore a year, expired on 31 December and the counterparty had its own logs. The DPDP rules limited what listening data Kahani could share to satisfy either an advertiser audit or a telecom partner without listener consent that it had not collected. Kavya's Android fix would ship on 22 September; the iOS investigation had not begun; and a corrected historical series was three weeks of work by a team of four in Bengaluru and Toronto whose working hours overlapped for ninety minutes a day.

10. Questions for discussion

Using Exhibits 1, 2 and 4, at what point, if any, did daily listening hours stop meeting each of these, and who in the company was in a position to know?

2. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 both appear to condemn autoplay and background playback, and both carry footnotes that undermine them. What can be concluded from each exhibit with confidence, what cannot, and what single piece of additional data would most change your reading?

3. Devika's candidate metric in Exhibit 6 comes from the same heartbeat stream as hours. Is it a better metric, a different metric, or the same metric with a lower ceiling? What would it take to make it one the board could adopt, and how long would that take?

5. Exhibit 5 shows that the same number is a contractual quantity for advertisers, a negotiating quantity for Al Madar, a vesting quantity for the founders, and an operating quantity for product. Can one definition serve all four, and if not, which should be split from the others first, and what does that do to the tranche clause?
